title: What to Send When You Start a Custom Software Project
description: Thinking about hiring a software shop in Idaho? Here's exactly what to put in your first note — no finished spec required, no prices or timelines needed.
author: Erik Short
markdown:
## Quick answers

**What should a business include in a custom software inquiry?** What the business does, where the current process breaks down, and who would actually use the new system day to day.
**Does a project have to start with a finished specification?** No. A rough, honest description of the problem is a better starting point than a polished spec written to guess at what a developer wants to hear.
**Do I need to know what the system should look like before reaching out?** No. That's part of the scoping conversation, not something you need to arrive with.
**Should I include numbers like budget or deadline in the first note?** Not required. What matters first is whether the problem is clear enough to scope.
**What if I only have a vague sense that "our spreadsheets aren't working"?** That's a completely normal starting point — describe what's going wrong in practice and the rest can get sorted out from there.

## The first note matters more than people think

Most people who reach out about custom software have never done it before. They're not sure what a software shop needs to hear, so they either write three paragraphs trying to sound technical, or they write one line — "need a system for tracking jobs" — and hope the rest gets figured out on a call.

Both are fine, honestly. But there's a version of that first note that gets a useful response back faster, and it's not about sounding technical at all. It's about being specific about three things: what the business does, where the current tools are failing, and who's actually going to use the thing once it exists.

That's it. No spec, no wireframes, no feature list required. Here's why those three things matter and how to write them.

## Tell us what the business actually does

This sounds obvious, but it gets skipped constantly. People write "we need a scheduling system" without saying what's being scheduled, for whom, or why the current way of doing it stopped working.

A dairy lab tracking samples, a general contractor dispatching crews, a youth sports league assigning umpires to games — these are all "scheduling systems" in some sense, but they have almost nothing in common underneath. The rules are different. The people involved are different. What counts as a conflict is different.

A couple sentences on the actual work is worth more than a page of requirements. Something like:

- What the business sells or does, in plain language
- Roughly how big the operation is — one location or several, a handful of people touching the system or dozens
- What makes this business's version of the problem different from the generic version (seasonal swings, multiple job sites, a regulatory requirement, whatever it is)

That context shapes everything downstream. It's the difference between a system that fits how the business actually runs and one that fits some generic idea of how a business like it is supposed to run.

## Say where the current tools are failing

This is the part that actually tells us what needs to get built. Not "we want a dashboard" — what's going wrong right now.

Common patterns worth naming:

- A spreadsheet that one person maintains and everyone else works around, because it's the only place the real numbers live
- Information that lives in email threads and text messages, so nobody has the full picture without asking around
- A process that worked fine at a smaller size and is now falling apart as the business has grown
- Double entry — the same information gets typed into two or three different places because nothing talks to anything else
- A deadline or compliance requirement that the current process can't reliably hit

If any of that sounds familiar, it's worth reading [our earlier post on outgrowing spreadsheets](/blog/when-a-treasure-valley-business-has-outgrown-its-spreadsheets) — it goes into more detail on the specific signs that a business has hit the ceiling of what a spreadsheet and some goodwill can do.

The goal here isn't to diagnose the technical solution yourself. It's to describe the pain clearly enough that someone else can see the shape of it. "Our dispatcher re-types every job into three different apps and still misses things" tells a developer a lot more than "we need better software."

## Say who will actually use it

A system gets built differently depending on who's sitting in front of it every day. A tool used by one office manager who's comfortable with computers is a different build than one used by thirty field techs on phones with gloves on, or by customers logging in themselves to check an order status.

Worth including:

- Who uses it internally, and roughly how many people
- Whether customers or outside partners will ever touch it directly, or if it's internal-only
- What devices people will actually be using — desk computer, phone, tablet in a truck
- Whether people need it to work without reliable internet, which comes up more than you'd think outside city centers

None of this requires guessing at technical architecture. It's just a description of the humans involved, and that description shapes real decisions — how simple the interface needs to be, whether it needs to work offline, whether notifications should go out by text instead of email. [SMS](/sms-signup) only gets set up when an operation actually needs it, and whether it does depends entirely on who's using the system and how.

## What you don't need to send

It's worth being just as clear about what's not required, because people often hold off reaching out because they think they need more than they do.

You don't need:

- A finished specification. A spec written by someone who's never done this before is usually a guess dressed up as a requirement, and it can do more harm than good if it locks in the wrong idea early.
- Wireframes or mockups. Those come out of the scoping conversation, not before it.
- A budget number, though it's fine to mention one if you have it.
- A deadline, though again, fine to mention if it's real and fixed.
- Technical vocabulary. "We need an API that integrates with our ERP" is fine if that's genuinely how you think about it, but "our accounting software and our scheduling spreadsheet don't talk to each other and someone has to retype everything" works just as well, maybe better.

A real project starts as a written scope — but that scope gets built together, after the first conversation, not handed over finished on day one. If you're trying to figure out whether a project like this is even the right move yet, or whether a smaller fix would do, that's a normal thing to sort out on the call too. Not every outgrown spreadsheet needs a full system built underneath it, and a shop worth hiring will tell you that instead of selling you more than the problem calls for.

## What a short, good inquiry actually looks like

Put together, a solid first note might read something like this:

> We run a small fleet of delivery trucks out of two locations in the Treasure Valley. Right now our drivers text in when a delivery's done, and our dispatcher manually updates a shared spreadsheet that customers sometimes ask to see. It's gotten harder to keep straight now that we've added a second location, and we've had a few deliveries that got double-counted or missed. We'd want our five drivers to be able to update status from their phones, and eventually let customers check order status themselves without calling in.

That's four sentences describing the business, two describing the breakdown, and two describing the people who'd use it. No spec. No mockups. No price. It's enough to start a real conversation.

## Frequently asked questions

### What should a business include in a custom software inquiry?
A plain description of what the business does, where the current process or tools are breaking down, and who would use the new system — how many people, in what roles, on what devices. That's enough to start a real conversation; the technical details get sorted out from there.

### Does a project have to start with a finished specification?
No. A written scope does come out of the process, but it's developed together after the first conversation, not handed in by the client on day one. Showing up with a clear description of the problem is more useful than showing up with a spec that guesses at the solution.

### How is a custom software project different from getting a website built?
A website is a marketing presence — built to be found and taken seriously, then handed over ready to use. Custom software is an internal system the business runs on day to day, like a job tracker or a customer portal, and it includes ongoing support after launch. They're separate offers because they solve different problems.

### What if I'm not sure whether we need custom software or just a better process?
That's a fair thing to not know yet, and it's worth raising directly in the first conversation. Sometimes the fix is smaller than a full system, and sometimes a spreadsheet really has been outgrown — [this post](/blog/when-a-treasure-valley-business-has-outgrown-its-spreadsheets) walks through some of the signs either way.

### Do I need to already have a budget or deadline in mind?
No. It's fine to mention either if they're real and fixed, but the first conversation is about understanding the problem clearly enough to scope it, not about matching a number.

If you've got a process that's held together with spreadsheets, texts, and someone's memory, [start the conversation](https://www.idsoftwaredev.com/#start) and tell us what's actually going wrong.
